text:
The passage rewards attention to what is missing. Sarah has no place in the chapter, and the book gives notice of her death in the verse that immediately follows it, Genesis 23:1. The scene does not state the matter; yet it implies that something in Abraham’s house did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants after the events on the mountain, but Isaac is not named among those who return (Genesis 22:19). At that exact point, where a lesser story would have lingered, the narrative turns away. Its silence is testimony, not blank absence.

An opposing reading is ready enough. The chapter, it may be said, merely observes the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains. This may, perhaps, in some sense, be true. Yet the narrator elsewhere names feeling plainly: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is therefore no accident. The narrator knows what has been withheld; in this narrative voice, restraint becomes a kind of accusation.
